To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of nitrogen and phosphorus losses from agricultural catchment occur as dissolved inorganic forms, but that the proportion of particulate and dissolved organic nitrogen and phosphorus is variable and may be significant.
The main sources of nitrogen and phosphorus loss in agricultural catchments are from agricultural land.
(1) the majority of N loss from agriculture occurs in the form of dissolved organic N (DON) and (2) that the majority of P loss is particulate in form.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) What is the magnitude of N and P loss from agricultural land and how is this related to land use, soil type and hydrological regime?

the development of a conceptual model of the cycling and fate of dissolved N and P species in agricultural drainage basins and with the development and application of new techniques for the measurement of these species in natural waters.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the spatial and temporal variability in the concentrations of all forms of nitrogen and phosphorus are very large, and that this variability is a result of both natural and anthropogenic processes.

the impact of agricultural land management on the flux of dissolved N and P from the land to receiving waters is highly variable and dependent on the nature of the land use, the soil type, the hydrology of the area, the nature and extent of the drainage network, the nutrient status of the soil, the nature and intensity of the fertilisation and the nature and extent and timing of the land management.
